Chinese cosmetics chase global growth as K‑beauty opens doors - CHOSUNBIZ 
 2026년 10월 27일(화) Industry Finance Real Estate IT Retail Science Policy Society International Entertainment Culture Sports English International Chinese cosmetics chase global growth as K‑beauty opens doors 
 Chinese beauty brands push into the US and Europe amid slow home demand, low name recognition, and geopolitical risks 
 입력 2026.10.27. 16:16 조선비즈 구글 검색 먼저 보기 Chinese cosmetics brands are accelerating their push into overseas markets such as the United States and Europe beyond their home market. They have secured a majority share at home by overtaking foreign brands, but with sluggish domestic demand persisting, they are seeking new growth engines. In particular, the overseas success of Korean cosmetics, known as K-beauty, is seen as having influenced Chinese companies' expansion abroad. However, low brand recognition and U.S.-China trade tensions are cited as obstacles.
 Illustration = ChatGPT According to Reuters on the 26th (local time), Proya, China's largest cosmetics brand by revenue, will sell skincare products starting next month at 400 stores and on the online mall of the U.S. cosmetics retailer Ulta Beauty (hereafter Ulta). Proya also established a research and development (R&D) center in Paris, France, this month.
 Other Chinese cosmetics brands are also increasing their overseas offline stores. Florasis opened its first overseas flagship store in Ginza, Tokyo, last year. Joocyee and Judydoll opened stores in Singapore last year. The two brands also entered Skin Cupid, a U.K.-based distributor specializing in Asian cosmetics.
 ◇ Led the Chinese cosmetics market, but seeking new growth engines
 Behind Chinese cosmetics companies turning to overseas markets are the competitiveness they have built at home and prolonged weak domestic demand. As Chinese cosmetics brands grew rapidly over the past decade, they changed the landscape of China's cosmetics market, which had been led by global brands.
 According to the China Association of Fragrance Flavor and Cosmetic Industries, Chinese cosmetics brands in 2022 surpassed the market share of foreign brands at home for the first time. In last year's $159 billion Chinese cosmetics market (about 210 trillion won), domestic brands' share reached 57.4%.
 However, with sluggish consumption in China continuing for years, Chinese cosmetics companies are seeking new revenue sources overseas. This push abroad extends beyond cosmetics to consumer goods overall, including fashion, electronics, and bubble tea.
 A shift in perceptions of Chinese-made products is also cited as a driving force behind overseas expansion. As Chinese corporations have established competitiveness in electric vehicles, smartphones, and artificial intelligence (AI), the evaluation of Chinese products in other industries is also changing, according to the Chinese industry.
 Proya, aiming to enter the world's top 10 cosmetics brands, is also considering acquisitions of small and midsize overseas cosmetics brands. Flower Knows, a color cosmetics brand in which Proya holds 51% equity, entered the U.K. cosmetics and healthcare retailer Boots in March and has been selling products in some U.S. Ulta stores since September.
 Visitors attend TikTok's K-beauty standalone TikTok Shop offline event Where Glow Begins in Shoreditch, London. The photo is unrelated to the article. /Courtesy of TikTok ◇ A path paved by K-beauty, with price competitiveness as a strength
 One of the cases Chinese cosmetics companies reference as they enter overseas markets is the success of K-beauty. Korean cosmetics have expanded their presence in the United States and Europe by promoting distinctive products and skincare routines. Korea's cosmetics exports totaled $11.4 billion (about 15 trillion won) last year, up 50% from five years earlier. According to the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC), Korea in 2024 overtook France to become the largest cosmetics exporter to the United States.
 Reuters analyzed that the success of K-beauty is having a positive impact on Chinese cosmetics companies' entry into overseas markets. As Korean cosmetics have raised overseas consumers' interest in Asian cosmetics, they have opened the door for Chinese brands to expand abroad.
 Jing An, an attorney at the New York law firm Altman & An, said K-beauty helped raise awareness of Asian culture in overseas markets. He said he has newly secured two Chinese cosmetics companies seeking to enter the U.S. over the past year as clients.
 In particular, the price competitiveness of Chinese cosmetics is expected to serve as a strength in overseas markets. With high inflation increasing consumers' price burden, relatively affordable Chinese cosmetics could emerge as a new option. Elisa Harca, co-founder of marketing firm Red Ant Asia, said, "Consumers around the world feel considerable fatigue with spending a lot of money on products they put on their skin."
 ◇ Overseas recognition is virtually "zero," settling in the market is key
 Low brand recognition in overseas markets is a challenge Chinese cosmetics companies must address. Proya founder and CEO Hou Junchen said at the recent opening ceremony for the Paris R&D center, "At present, Proya's brand recognition in Europe and the United States is essentially zero (0)," adding, "We will work with partners to earn consumers' trust and lead that to product purchases."
 Marc-Antoine Jamet, chairman of Cosmetic Valley, a French cosmetics industry group, gave a positive assessment of Proya's growth potential. He said Proya has expanded from the mass market to the premium market, adding, "I don't know whether it will take six weeks, six months, or six years, but (Proya) will enter the high-end cosmetics market."
 U.S.-China trade frictions and geopolitical tensions are expected to be variables in Chinese cosmetics companies' expansion into overseas markets. Whether Chinese brands can carry over the competitiveness they have built at home to foreign markets appears to depend on how well they overcome these uncertainties.
